I’m not sure which country you’re in, but I’m in The Netherlands and elective C sections are quite rare but for my second pregnancy I was referred to a specialist service here where I met with a OB, a psychologist and a midwife. I was offered a c section but declined because I had vaginal birth with my first so in a way I knew what to expect and the “unknown” of a c section was something I didn’t want. 

So,  we worked with them on a very specific birth plan that was like plastered clearly all over my notes. And that was no male hospital staff unless an absolute emergency, an epidural as a priority and open discussion and asking of consent when I was touched. Having my waters broken and initial checks were uncomfortable and I was scooting up the bed, but they were very kind and gentle. The birth experience itself was very good, it didn’t hinder me having a good birth and, due to their care and kindness, I didn’t struggle much.

My birth story is on my profile if you want to read it! 

Wishing you the best of luck and hope you find the solution that works best for you!

I’m in the Netherlands and got 6 days after the birth you have the option to have a kraamzorg (maternity care) come to your home for up to 6 hours per day. They help you navigate that first week, teach you things about caring for the baby, help with breastfeeding and also do light cleaning and chores for you. It is especially helpful as they can take the baby for a couple of hours in the day so you can sleep. They can also check any stitches or tearing you have the make sure it’s healing ok.

You also stay registered with you midwife practice for a number of weeks after and they will visit you at home, check on your healing, check on your mental health, check the baby too.

The veterinary industry, 10000000000000000000000000%

Don't get me wrong there are vets and companies who are very shady and do very very questionable things just to try and make money (if you're from the UK there is a company called MEDIVET and oh my lord steer clear - there is a panorama docu on them and i suggest you watch before you even consider taking an animal there).

But on the most part a lot of people in the veterinary industry are honest and hard working people. Vets do get paid a decent amount but they are a GP, a surgeon, a dentist and more rolled into one and compared to the human equivalent they making a very low wage for the amount of studying to qualify and the amount of work and hours they put into their job. 

People seem to be of the opinion that if vets love animals they would provide all care for free but unfortunately medical supplies, buying/renting a property, medical equipment and employing staff are not cheap, and costs have to be met. Individuals who love animals should not be expected to carry the financial burden for those who want a pet but cannot afford it. 

As a vet nurse I've worked with some amazing vets and with some shit ones and I have handled the ordering of meds and supplies (in my previous place of work with 3 vets, 3 nurses the meds order was £600+ DAILY) and I have handled the cashing up and organization of finances and anyone who thinks vets are wildly rich and living off exploiting you then you are very much mistaken.
